column1: What causes lock blocking in SQL Server?
column2:
A session waits for an incompatible lock held by another session.
A lock protects data against incompatible operations. For example, a writer can hold a lock that prevents another writer from changing the same row. The second writer can proceed once the lock is released.
Review source

column1: What distinguishes a lock deadlock from ordinary blocking?
column2:
A cycle of dependencies prevents the participating transactions from proceeding.
Ordinary blocking only needs one session to wait. In a deadlock, each participant in a cycle needs something another participant holds, so SQL Server rolls back one transaction to let work continue.
Review source

column1: In a chain of sessions waiting on locks, how do you find the head blocker?
column2:
Follow blocking session IDs to the session that blocks others without being blocked.
Start with a waiting request and follow its blocking session ID to the next session. Repeat until you find the session at the head of the chain. It can be idle and still hold locks.
Review source

column1: Why can a sleeping session block other transactions despite having no active request?
column2:
It can retain an uncommitted transaction and its locks.
A sleeping session runs no current request, but it can still own locks from an earlier statement in an open transaction. A request-only view can miss it, so inspect the corresponding session and transaction information.
Review source

column1: After a statement times out, what must an application do with an open transaction it intends to abandon?
column2:
Roll back any abandoned transaction that remains open.
A timeout or cancellation can stop the current statement without rolling back an explicit transaction. If the application will abandon the work, it must clean up the transaction before reusing the connection.
Review source

column1: Under locking reads, how can an application that stops fetching results prolong blocking?
column2:
The unfinished request can retain locks while waiting for the client.
If the client stops reading rows, the server can wait for it to accept more results. Under locking reads, a request that has not finished can hold locks longer and delay other work.
Review source

column1: Before terminating a SQL Server blocker, what must you establish about its open transaction?
column2:
Whether its transaction is progressing or is genuinely abandoned.
Identify the owner and check whether the transaction is active or abandoned. Terminating it cancels its work and triggers rollback, which can continue to hold up other requests until cleanup finishes.
Review source

column1: What is the normal response when a blocking SQL Server session is already rolling back its transaction?
column2:
Allow the rollback to finish.
Rollback is already undoing the incomplete transaction. Repeating KILL does not make that work finish faster. Accelerated database recovery can reduce rollback time in Azure SQL Database.
Review source

column1: Why keep user input and external service calls outside database transactions?
column2:
They prolong the transaction and can extend blocking.
Locks held until transaction end can remain during a user pause or a slow service request. Move that waiting outside the transaction so the database finishes its protected work sooner.
Review source

column1: Under Azure SQL Database optimized locking and versioned READ COMMITTED reads, how can writers still block each other?
column2:
One writer can wait for another writer's uncommitted changes.
Versioned reads reduce reader-writer conflicts, but two transactions still cannot freely change the same row. A writer can wait on the first transaction's transaction ID lock until that transaction finishes.
Review source

column1: What criteria does SQL Server use to choose which transaction to roll back in a deadlock?
column2:
Lower deadlock priority first, then lower rollback cost when priorities are equal.
Deadlock priority is considered before cost. If the priorities match, SQL Server favors rolling back the transaction estimated to require less undo work. If both values match, it can choose either victim.
Review source

column1: What must an application retry after its transaction becomes a deadlock victim?
column2:
The entire transaction, not just its last statement.
SQL Server rolls back the victim transaction, including successful statements that ran before the deadlock. Retrying only the final statement can leave the earlier changes missing and break the original unit of work.
Review source

column1: Why add a short randomized delay before retrying a deadlock victim's transaction?
column2:
To reduce the chance that the same transactions collide again immediately.
A random delay spreads out retries so the same sessions are less likely to meet again immediately. A bounded retry can recover a request, but recurring deadlocks still need investigation.
Review source

column1: How does accessing shared objects in a consistent order reduce deadlocks?
column2:
It reduces circular lock dependencies between transactions.
If both transactions access A before B, one can wait for A before holding B. That removes this particular A-then-B versus B-then-A cycle, but other access patterns can still deadlock.
Review source

column1: How can an appropriate index reduce blocking and deadlocks?
column2:
It can reduce the data accessed and the duration of lock conflicts.
A suitable index can help an operation find its rows without scanning unrelated data. This can shorten the operation or reduce lock conflicts. Test with the real queries because additional indexes also require work on writes.
Review source

column1: When can Query Store plan forcing help reduce recurring deadlocks?
column2:
When a particular execution plan causes the problematic access pattern.
A different plan can change the order or number of rows accessed. If history shows the deadlocks started with a plan change, test a previously stable plan and monitor results while you investigate.
Review source

column1: Which built-in Extended Events session captures deadlock graphs in SQL Server and Azure SQL Managed Instance?
column2:
system_health.
The built-in system_health session captures the XML deadlock report on these platforms. Azure SQL Database does not provide that built-in session, so capture the database-level event in a custom session there.
Review source

column1: Which section of a deadlock graph shows lock owners and waiters for each resource?
column2:
resource-list.
The resource list shows what each participant owns and what another participant wants. Match process identifiers to the process list to connect those lock relationships to the statements in the cycle.
Review source

column1: Why use an event_file target instead of a ring buffer for durable Azure SQL deadlock history?
column2:
The ring buffer loses its events when the event session stops.
An in-memory ring buffer can lose older events and clears when the session stops. An event file writes the events to Azure Storage, so they can be reviewed after the session stops.
Review source

column1: When Azure SQL Database reports a deadlock, what has the engine already done to resolve it?
column2:
The engine already chose a victim and broke the cycle.
The alert reports that a deadlock occurred. SQL Server already chose a victim to resolve that cycle. The useful next step is to examine captured deadlock graphs for a repeated pattern.
Review source

column1: In a CATCH block that owns the transaction, how do you roll back only if a transaction remains?
column2:
IF XACT_STATE() <> 0 ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
XACT_STATE() returns zero when no user transaction is active. A deadlock victim's transaction can already be gone, so rollback only when the transaction-owning error handler still has a transaction to clean up.
Review source
